India has entered the second half of the 2020s carrying a striking and uncomfortable political reality: protest has become one of the most visible languages through which citizens communicate dissatisfaction with the state, institutions, political parties, markets and public systems. Over roughly the last decade, from 2016 through 2025, India has witnessed an extraordinary succession of demonstrations involving farmers, students, unemployed youth, workers, doctors, athletes, women, caste groups, religious communities, consumers, civil-society organisations and political parties. These movements have not all had the same ideology, objective or political direction, and it would be inaccurate to describe every demonstration as an anti-government movement. Some have demanded reservations, some protection of constitutional rights, some better crop prices, some employment, some justice after crimes, some changes in examination systems, and others have opposed particular laws or administrative decisions. Yet taken together, they reveal something important: a large section of Indian society increasingly believes that when ordinary institutional channels fail to produce a satisfactory response, the street becomes the final available forum for being heard. The scale of this phenomenon is not merely anecdotal. The Armed Conflict Location & Event Data project, which tracks demonstrations, found India to be one of the world's most protest-intensive countries and recorded 14,784 demonstrations in India in 2018 alone. Its analysis also found that demonstrations involved an unusually wide range of groups, including political parties, labour organisations, students, teachers, farmers, caste groups, health workers, religious groups and journalists.

The significance of the last ten years therefore lies not in one particular protest but in the accumulation of grievances. A society does not repeatedly send farmers onto highways, students onto university campuses, job aspirants into examination centres and streets, doctors into demonstrations, athletes to public squares and citizens into marches for exactly the same reason. Each movement has its own immediate trigger, but underneath them are recurring questions about accountability, fairness, opportunity, institutional competence and the ability of the government to listen. The question is not simply whether India has protests; a democracy will naturally have protests. The more important question is why so many different social groups repeatedly conclude that protest is necessary before the administration, political leadership or institutions respond. That distinction is crucial. Public protest is not automatically proof of government failure, just as the absence of protest is not proof of good governance. But repeated protest across unrelated sectors can be understood as an indicator of accumulated social pressure and declining confidence in ordinary mechanisms of redress.

The year 2016 offered an early warning of this pattern. Haryana witnessed a major Jat reservation agitation that paralysed parts of the state, disrupted transport and affected Delhi's water supply. The movement was rooted in demands for reservation in government employment and education, reflecting the extraordinary competition surrounding public-sector opportunities. Reuters reported that the protests resulted in at least 16 deaths and eventually ended after the government gave assurances concerning employment reservations. The episode demonstrated that the employment problem in India was not simply about the official unemployment rate. It was also about the extraordinary value attached to a limited number of secure government positions. When millions compete for a relatively small pool of stable employment, reservation, recruitment rules, examination procedures and government vacancies can become politically explosive issues.

The same period also saw the JNU controversy and student mobilisation, protests surrounding universities and questions about nationalism, freedom of expression and the use of state power. At the same time, there were protests connected to demonetisation and its economic consequences, with political parties and citizen groups challenging the government's decision and its implementation. These events were important because they showed that protest in India was becoming simultaneously social, political and digital. Demonstrations were no longer confined to traditional labour unions or established political organisations. Students, social-media users, professionals and informal networks could rapidly turn a local grievance into a national political argument.

In 2017, the extraordinary mobilisation around Jallikattu in Tamil Nadu demonstrated another dimension of Indian protest culture. What began as opposition to restrictions on the traditional bull-taming sport developed into a huge youth-led movement. The protest was not simply a conventional left-versus-right political confrontation. It involved questions of cultural identity, federalism, judicial intervention and the feeling among young people that decisions affecting local traditions were being made without sufficient public participation. The Jallikattu movement was particularly significant because it demonstrated the ability of digitally connected young Indians to create mass mobilisation without depending entirely on conventional political parties. ACLED identifies January 2017 as one of the major spikes in Indian demonstration activity since 2016.

The year 2018 was even more revealing. India recorded 14,784 demonstrations according to ACLED, nearly three times the number recorded in Pakistan in the same dataset. Demonstration activity expanded substantially, and India was identified as one of the countries with the highest number of demonstrations globally. The year included the Bharat Bandh associated with anger over the Supreme Court's interpretation of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, large-scale Maratha reservation protests, farmers' marches, protests over the Sterlite copper plant in Tamil Nadu and numerous other regional movements. ACLED's research shows that protest in India was geographically broad, with more than half of demonstrations occurring in North India, roughly one-third in South India and the remainder in eastern parts of the country. This is important because it demonstrates that public dissatisfaction cannot be reduced to a single region, religion, caste or political ideology.

The Sterlite episode in Tamil Nadu, the farmers' mobilisations in several states and the continuing reservation movements also exposed a recurring problem in Indian governance: development decisions often create a conflict between national or economic objectives and the immediate interests of communities. Industrial projects promise investment and employment but may create environmental, health or livelihood concerns. Infrastructure promises connectivity but can involve land acquisition and displacement. Reservation policies seek social justice but operate within a fiercely competitive employment market. Each side can possess legitimate arguments, yet when consultation, transparency and institutional trust are weak, policy disagreements can rapidly become street conflicts.

By 2019, the centre of national protest politics shifted dramatically toward citizenship, constitutional identity and questions surrounding the relationship between the individual and the state. The Citizenship Amendment Act, combined with fears and controversies surrounding the proposed National Register of Citizens, generated a nationwide movement beginning in late 2019 and continuing into 2020. Students, women, civil-society groups and ordinary citizens participated in demonstrations, with Shaheen Bagh becoming an international symbol of prolonged citizen-led protest. The movement was especially significant because its participants were not primarily demanding wages, subsidies or government jobs. They were contesting the perceived implications of government policy for citizenship, equality and constitutional secularism. The protests also produced serious clashes and deaths, while authorities in several areas imposed restrictions on assembly and internet services. Reuters has described the CAA protests as one of the major mass movements of the period, alongside the farmers' movement and other major national protests.

The CAA controversy also illustrated another feature of the contemporary Indian protest environment: the widening gap between competing perceptions of the same government policy. Supporters argued that the law provided protection to persecuted minorities from neighbouring countries, while opponents argued that religion had been introduced into a citizenship framework in a manner inconsistent with constitutional equality. The resulting dispute became much larger than the legislation itself. It became a debate about the meaning of Indian citizenship, the secular character of the republic, the role of police power and the legitimacy of dissent. That is why the protests remained politically powerful even after the immediate legislative controversy had faded.

Then came 2020, a year in which India's social and economic pressures were intensified by the COVID-19 pandemic. The lockdown produced an unprecedented humanitarian and economic shock, particularly for migrant workers and informal-sector households. Millions of workers were stranded or forced to undertake long journeys to return to their home states. The pandemic also created tensions over lockdown restrictions, livelihoods, health systems and access to essential services. At the same time, another protest movement was beginning that would eventually become one of the largest and most consequential in modern Indian history: the farmers' protest against the three agricultural laws.

The 2020–21 farmers' movement represented a fundamental challenge to the government's claim that its agricultural reforms would modernise markets and benefit farmers. Farmer organisations, particularly from Punjab and Haryana and subsequently from other parts of India, argued that the reforms threatened the existing procurement system and could weaken the economic security provided by minimum support prices. The movement evolved into a year-long mobilisation around Delhi, involving road blockades, tractor marches, mass gatherings and negotiations with the government. Eventually, Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced the repeal of the three farm laws in November 2021. Reuters has described the movement as a year-long protest that ultimately forced the government to withdraw the legislation.

The farmers' movement was a turning point because it demonstrated that even a government possessing a strong parliamentary majority could be compelled to reverse a major policy when a sufficiently large and organised social constituency refused to accept it. The lesson was not necessarily that the agricultural reforms were inherently wrong or that every farmer's argument was correct. The deeper lesson was that policy legitimacy requires more than legislative majority. A government may possess the constitutional authority to enact a law, but durable policy also requires social acceptance, consultation and trust. Where a significant affected community believes that the government has not adequately addressed its concerns, the formal legality of a decision does not automatically produce political legitimacy.

The year 2021 also exposed the fragility of public confidence in institutions. The farmers' protest continued for much of the year, while students and job aspirants remained concerned about recruitment examinations and delayed vacancies. The pandemic had already interrupted education, employment and household incomes. The economic recovery that followed was uneven across sectors and social groups. For millions of young people, especially those preparing for competitive examinations, the promise of education leading to stable employment increasingly appeared uncertain. The problem was not only unemployment in the statistical sense; it was the years of preparation, coaching fees, examination delays, cancelled examinations, changing eligibility criteria and repeated uncertainty that produced frustration.

In 2022, the Agnipath military recruitment scheme triggered another nationwide youth mobilisation. Young people protested against the government's plan to recruit soldiers for shorter terms under the new Agniveer system. Demonstrations and railway disruptions occurred in several states. The protesters' concern was fundamentally economic and professional: military service had traditionally been viewed by many families as a source of stable employment, social status and long-term security, while the new short-term structure changed that expectation. The government defended the reform as necessary to make the armed forces younger and reduce pension expenditure, while critics argued that four years of service followed by uncertainty for most recruits would leave young people without sufficient long-term employment security. Reuters identifies the 2022 Agnipath protests as another major episode in India's recent cycle of mass mobilisation.

This episode is particularly important when viewed alongside the earlier Jat reservation protests and the later examination controversies. Across different communities, a common concern appears repeatedly: the competition for secure employment is becoming so intense that changes in recruitment rules can produce immediate social unrest. India has one of the world's largest young populations, and the demographic dividend becomes a political liability if education expands faster than the availability of productive, adequately paid and secure employment. The problem becomes even sharper when government employment is disproportionately attractive because private-sector jobs are perceived as unstable, poorly paid or lacking social security.

The year 2023 brought another set of protests that revealed the growing demand for institutional accountability. India's leading wrestlers, including Olympic medallists, demonstrated in Delhi against Wrestling Federation of India president Brij Bhushan Sharan Singh, whom they accused of sexually harassing female athletes. Singh denied the allegations. The wrestlers demanded investigation and action, and their protest continued for months. Reuters reported that the athletes suspended their protest after receiving assurances of a swift investigation, while several protesters had earlier been detained when the protest site was cleared.

The wrestlers' movement became significant because it crossed the boundary between sport and governance. These were not anonymous protesters. They were athletes who had represented India internationally and won medals for the country. Their decision to sit on the streets communicated a powerful message: national achievement does not necessarily translate into institutional protection. Their protest also raised the broader question of whether powerful individuals connected to political institutions receive different treatment from ordinary citizens. Whatever the eventual legal conclusions in an individual case, the political significance of the movement lay in its demand that institutional processes be visibly independent, credible and accessible.

The same year, the Manipur crisis exposed a very different but even more serious dimension of unrest: prolonged ethnic conflict and the inability of political institutions to restore social peace. Violence began in May 2023 after protests connected to demands for Scheduled Tribe status for the Meitei community and rapidly escalated into conflict involving Meitei and Kuki communities. By late 2024, Reuters reported that the conflict had resulted in around 260 deaths and the displacement of more than 60,000 people, with the violence continuing despite security deployments and political intervention.

Manipur demonstrates why the word "protest" must not be used as a catch-all description for every form of unrest. Peaceful demonstrations, civil disobedience, communal violence, insurgency, ethnic conflict and riots are different phenomena. They may share grievances but require completely different policy responses. A democratic state must protect peaceful dissent while simultaneously preventing violence and protecting citizens from harm. The challenge becomes particularly severe when citizens lose faith in the neutrality of the police or administration. In such circumstances, every administrative action can itself become a source of suspicion.

In 2024, the cycle intensified again. Farmers returned to the roads demanding legally guaranteed minimum support prices and other agricultural reforms. Thousands of farmers from Punjab began another Delhi Chalo march in February, and security forces used tear gas and water cannons to stop the march near the Punjab-Haryana border. Reuters reported that farmers were demanding legally backed guarantees for crop prices and arguing that their incomes remained under pressure. The renewed mobilisation was politically significant because it demonstrated that the repeal of the three farm laws in 2021 had not resolved the broader agricultural crisis.

The 2024 farmers' movement therefore revealed an important distinction between resolving a protest and resolving a grievance. A government can withdraw a particular law and thereby end one protest, but if the underlying economic problem remains, the issue can return in another form. Farmers were no longer primarily fighting the three repealed agricultural laws. They were demanding a legal guarantee of minimum prices, debt relief and broader economic security. The protest thus moved from opposition to a specific policy toward a demand for structural economic assurance.

The most politically explosive issue of 2024, however, was arguably the examination and recruitment crisis. The controversy surrounding NEET-UG and other competitive examinations produced anger among students, parents and job aspirants. Questions were raised about paper leaks, irregularities, grace marks, examination centres, examination administration and the fairness of competitive selection. The problem was especially serious because competitive examinations are not ordinary tests for millions of Indian families. They represent years of preparation, substantial coaching expenditure and, in many cases, the primary route to medical education or government employment. When candidates believe the examination system itself is compromised, the entire promise of merit becomes questionable.

The examination crisis exposed an especially dangerous form of institutional failure: a failure that directly attacks the belief that effort is rewarded fairly. A young person can tolerate failure if the examination is believed to be honest. A candidate can accept not getting a government job if the selection process appears transparent. But if candidates believe that papers can be leaked, answers manipulated, results altered or powerful candidates receive preferential treatment, frustration changes character. It is no longer simply disappointment. It becomes a perception that the system itself is unfair.

This is why paper leaks and recruitment scandals have generated such strong reactions across India. The problem extends beyond NEET. Over the past decade, different states have faced controversies involving recruitment examinations, question-paper leaks, delayed examinations and cancellations. For a generation raised on the promise that education is the route to social mobility, examination integrity is a foundational issue. When that foundation is shaken, anger naturally moves from the examination centre to the government department, the recruiting agency and eventually the political system.

The 2024 protests following the rape and murder of a trainee doctor at R.G. Kar Medical College and Hospital in Kolkata further broadened the protest landscape. Doctors and medical workers across India demonstrated over workplace safety, justice and institutional accountability. Reuters has identified the nationwide doctors' protests following the Kolkata case as one of the major mass movements of the period. The movement was not merely about one criminal case. It reflected a much broader concern over the safety of women, the working conditions of healthcare professionals and the ability of institutions to protect people who work inside public systems.

At the same time, the public debate increasingly expanded toward the cost of living. Petrol and diesel prices, food inflation, cooking costs, school fees, healthcare expenses, housing costs and household debt have all become politically sensitive subjects. Inflation is not experienced by citizens as an abstract percentage announced by a statistical agency. It is experienced when the monthly grocery bill rises, when commuting costs increase, when a family cannot afford private medical treatment, or when education and coaching consume a growing share of household income. In August 2026, for example, India's retail inflation was reported at 4.45% year-on-year, with food inflation at 5.52%, illustrating why price pressures remain politically relevant even when headline inflation remains within the Reserve Bank of India's tolerance band.

The politics of fuel prices also illustrates the complexity of governance. India remains heavily dependent on imported energy, meaning international oil prices, currency movements, taxes and domestic pricing decisions all affect consumers. Citizens, however, experience the final retail price rather than the underlying global economic explanation. When petrol becomes expensive, the political question is immediate: why should the ordinary consumer bear the burden? When prices fall, citizens ask why the reduction is not fully transmitted to retail markets. The same tension applies to electricity, transport, food and other essential services.

Infrastructure has created another source of public anger. India has undeniably constructed enormous quantities of roads, highways, airports, railways, bridges and other infrastructure over the past decade, so the claim that "development is nil" would be factually incorrect. The more serious issue is the quality, safety, planning and accountability of development. A road can be built but poorly maintained. A bridge can be inaugurated but lack adequate approaches. A project can receive funding but face land-acquisition delays. A highway can improve connectivity but still have dangerous design flaws. The Comptroller and Auditor General has repeatedly identified problems involving planning, procurement, execution, land acquisition, cost and utilisation in infrastructure projects. In one CAG audit, for example, 15 bridges costing ₹146.06 crore were found to have become disconnected from the relevant road alignment, while numerous other bridges lacked connectivity because of land and construction issues.

The issue therefore is not whether India has developed; it clearly has. The issue is whether development is sufficiently reliable, safe, equitable and accountable. Recent bridge collapses, tunnel accidents, road failures and infrastructure-related deaths have repeatedly produced public questions about construction standards, inspection systems, contractor accountability and political pressure to inaugurate projects before all associated work is complete. When infrastructure fails, citizens do not experience it as an accounting irregularity. They experience it through accidents, deaths, lost livelihoods and disrupted travel. The 2023 Uttarakhand tunnel collapse, in which 41 workers were trapped for 17 days, and subsequent infrastructure accidents have kept these questions alive.

The Comptroller and Auditor General's reports are particularly important in this discussion because CAG is a constitutional audit institution rather than a political opposition party. Its reports have repeatedly examined expenditure, implementation and compliance across government programmes. Its database includes audits covering Bharatmala, railways, roads, toll operations, aviation, healthcare, social welfare and numerous state programmes. The existence of a CAG observation does not automatically establish corruption or criminal wrongdoing; an audit finding can represent an irregularity, weakness in procedure, poor planning or financial-management problem. But repeated audit observations demonstrate why citizens demand stronger mechanisms to ensure that public money produces measurable public value.

🇮🇳 Salute to our security forces.

In a coordinated multi-state operation on Aug 12, 2026, Indian agencies dismantled the ISI-backed Shahzad Bhatti Network (SBN) — a Pakistan-run terror syndicate — just days before Independence Day, thwarting what could’ve been a coordinated wave of attacks on Indian soil.

📊 The numbers: • 253 detained across 14 states — UP (62), Haryana (52), Delhi (51), Punjab (44), Rajasthan (15), Maharashtra (8), Uttarakhand (5), Karnataka/Gujarat/Bihar (3 each), Telangana/HP/J&K/Kerala (2 each) • 80+ FIRs, 200+ arrests under UAPA, BNS, Arms Act, NDPS Act & Explosive Substances Act • Recoveries: IEDs, grenades with Pakistan Ordnance Factory markings, pistols, live cartridges, espionage CCTVs

Shahzad Bhatti — a Pakistan-based, ISI-backed handler — built a decentralised terror ecosystem inside India using local recruits and sleeper cells. He’s already linked by NIA to the Jalandhar grenade attack (Mar 2025), the Sirsa Women’s PS blast (Nov 2025), and the Ambala car-bomb case (Jan 2026), in which he and 7 Indians were chargesheeted.

The most dangerous part: recruitment happened through social media and encrypted apps — ordinary Indian youth lured with money to do recon, plant devices, and install spy cameras, often without knowing who they were really working for.

This is why this kind of coordinated, silent, relentless work by our NIA, State Police and ATS teams deserves real recognition. Deep respect to every officer — known and unnamed — who worked around the clock to keep us safe. 🙏

But busting one network isn’t a permanent fix. If Indians can be radicalised and recruited from their own phones, we need policy, not just case-by-case busts:

👉 A strict digital firewall on Pakistani-origin channels, apps and content reaching Indian users 

👉 Active government monitoring of foreign digital traffic entering India 

👉 Tighter regulation so ISI-linked handlers can’t keep exploiting Instagram/WhatsApp to groom our youth

Did Meta Make A Big Mistake By Removing PM Modi's Video??
- Amit Dubey

Meta did make a major error by temporarily removing Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Facebook video, a move that sparked intense governmental backlash and severe legal warnings in India. In an interview on the channel of popular digital creator RJRaunac, cyber security expert Amit Dubey highlighted how this incident exposed deep flaws in how big tech operates.

PM Modi posted a video on July 23 addressing Gen Z students about the NEET paper leak controversy. The video was suddenly blocked and remained unavailable on Facebook for over five hours.

Meta initially cited legal obligations, but later blamed an automated AI filter glitch for the accidental takedown.

The Indian government and a parliamentary IT panel, led by MP Nishikant Dubey, heavily grilled Meta's global team. They rejected the "technical glitch" excuse, raising questions about potential algorithmic bias and systemic flaws.

Loss of Safe Harbour Protection: The Parliamentary Committee warned Meta that it could lose its "safe harbour" immunity under Section 79 of the IT Act if accountability isn't met. This protection shields Meta from legal liability for user-generated content; losing it would expose the company to massive legal vulnerabilities.

Demand for Zuckerberg's Apology: While Meta's Global Affairs chief Joel Kaplan conveyed an official apology to IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw, the parliamentary panel has heavily pushed for a personal, written apology from Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg.

The incident has significantly damaged Meta’s standing in India its largest global user market reigniting intense national debates around digital sovereignty and the lack of human transparency in big-tech content moderation.

🌍Let's understand the background -- India has a fake-website problem. For years, fraudsters have registered domains impersonating global brands -- bogus Amazon shopping sites, fake McDonald's franchise offers, phony Microsoft support pages -- to con ordinary people. Dozens of companies took them to court.

🌍 What happened in December 2025? a Delhi judge cracked down. She blocked more than 1,100 fraudulent sites. But she didn't stop there.

She wrote sweeping new rules for the entire domain industry: strip away privacy protection by default, hand over website owners' details within 72 hours to anyone claiming a "legitimate interest," and block any web address resembling a protected brand.

Its warning is striking: the rules would make the internet less safe, not more. They'd expose ordinary website owners to stalking and harassment. And because domain systems are global, an order from one Delhi courtroom could ripple across the entire web -- potentially forcing GoDaddy to "exit India" altogether.

🌍 They are colourful filings: One of GoDaddy's arguments? That you can't ban the word "McDonald" -- it's a Scottish surname meaning "son of the world ruler."  The U.S. giant also submitted research compiled from the Merriam-Webster's website to argue that safeguarding variations of a protected trademark like "HUL" - Unilever's Indian unit, could overlap with 118 English words that contain the string, like "hulk" and "moghul".

GoDaddy has challenged a Delhi High Court order that it says could reshape how the internet works far beyond India.

In December, the court blocked more than 1,100 fake websites impersonating brands like Amazon, McDonald's and Microsoft. But the ruling went further, issuing 14 directives that tech experts say rewrite the rules of internet governance. Domain sellers can no longer offer free privacy protection by default. A website owner's name, address, phone and email must be released to anyone with a "legitimate interest" within 72 hours. Domain names resembling protected brand names are prohibited outright.

GoDaddy, which manages 80 million domains for over 20 million customers, has filed a 5,121-page appeal arguing the order conflicts with India's own data protection law and the EU's GDPR. It warns the directives are commercially destabilising enough to force domain companies to exit India. Namecheap and Hosting Concepts have filed their own challenges.

India's concern is grounded in a real crisis. The government received 2.4 million cybercrime complaints last year involving losses of 2.4 billion dollars, and the Home Minister has said one person falls victim to cybercrime every 37 seconds. Court records show the directives closely followed submissions by the IT and home ministries.

Internet governance researchers warn the people exposed by public registration data will be journalists, activists and small business owners rather than fraudsters. GoDaddy points to a practical problem: protecting a trademark like HUL would overlap with 118 English words, including hulk and moghul.

A larger bench hears the appeals on July 16. A domestic anti-fraud ruling is quietly becoming a global internet governance precedent.

Most of these directions were issued through the Sahyog portal, a government platform used by Central and state agencies to send blocking notices to social media companies. Digital-rights advocates have raised concerns about this mechanism and its implications for due process and freedom of expression.

Earlier in its brief existence, the site was live and then responded with standard HTTP 403 errors from Hostinger’s active servers before the hold took effect.

In domain management terms, “clientHold” is a standard EPP (Extensible Provisioning Protocol) status code controlled exclusively by the registrar, not by governments or external authorities. According to ICANN documentation and registrar policies, this status instructs the registry not to publish the domain in the DNS, effectively taking it offline until the registrar resolves the underlying issue. Such instruction can be issued only by the owner of the website, not third parties, not even governments. Alternately, the domain provider or the host can take the website offline due to various reasons.

It is commonly applied for routine administrative reasons such as incomplete WHOIS contact verification, billing or payment problems, compliance violations, or at the request of the domain owner. The clientHold affects resolution globally at the registry level, not at any country level.

On the other hand, when a government orders blocking a website, it is done through ISPs (Internet Service Providers) in the country, and the block only takes place in that country. In India, such a block is typically enforced through the Department of Telecommunications via ISP-level DNS poisoning, IP blacklisting, or URL filtering. Such actions allow the domain to still resolve correctly on international resolvers outside the country. That is why websites blocked by the Indian govt can be accessed in India through VPN.

Moreover, when one visits a website blocked by the govt, the browser displays a message saying the same. But when one visits cockroachjantaparty’s website, the browser displays the code DNS_PROBE_FINISHED_NXDOMAIN. This means the browser can’t find the domain because it has been deactivated.

Moreover, no public government orders, court directives, or official statements have been issued regarding https://t.co/n5u5L8JbZ5, further undermining the censorship claim.

Therefore, the analysis of the website shows that either it has been taken by Dipte himself, or the domain provider/host took it down due to some compliance issues. There is no evidence that the site was taken down on Indian government’s order.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

*STATEMENT: Escalating Digital Censorship in India*

*New Delhi, February 28, 2026*

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by a cluster of online blocking and takedown actions and ISP level service disruptions reported between 24–28 February 2026. Across these incidents, users and affected services face restrictions without clear, timely reasons and without access to the underlying orders needed to challenge state action by exercising their rights to obtain legal remedy.

Developers reported severe, uneven disruption in access to Supabase across multiple Indian networks. Reporting indicates the disruption followed a government direction, with accounts suggesting use of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Yet there has been no public statement of the grounds, scope, or duration, and no accessible order for those impacted. Supabase has publicly stated that its domains became inaccessible due to a “ministry order”, and users have been pushed to workarounds such as alternative DNS or VPNs. In parallel, users on X (formerly Twitter) continue to receive “withheld in India” notices restricting specific posts within the country. Such notices usually do not provide the government order or its reasoning. Hence, for those who are being censored the basics of natural justice of a notice, opportunity for a hearing and remedy are delayed or absent.

This is enabled by secrecy built into the blocking framework. Section 69A is implemented through the 2009 Blocking Rules, which contemplate a committee process and, where feasible, notice to intermediaries and identifiable originators. But they also impose “strict confidentiality” over requests and actions taken. When orders and reasons are secret by default, affected persons cannot test legality, necessity, proportionality, or factual errors except through protracted litigation. When in _Shreya Singhal v. Union of India_ (2015), the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A while relying on the existence of procedural safeguards and reasoned decisions, indicating that impacted users could approach court in writ remedies. However, due to the operational secrecy and providing copies of orders and notices those who are censored and prevented from obtaining judicial remedy.

The February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules, 2021 further increase these risks. The substituted Rule 3(1)(d) requires intermediaries to remove or disable access within three hours of receiving “actual knowledge”, which can arise from a court order or a written “reasoned intimation” by authorised government officers. While the rule lists what a “reasoned intimation” should contain, the legal basis, statutory provision, nature of the unlawful act, and specific URL/identifier, the three-hour window pressures platforms to comply promptly which may often occur without any substantive assessment. These inherently opaque censorship practices are being accelerated through "Sahyog" portal. Developed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the Sahyog portal operates entirely without statutory footing, only being anchored in the IT Rules, 2021 that are created by executive notification. It functions as a censorship clearinghouse that deliberately bypasses the established, albeit weak, procedural safeguards of Section 69A. By routing automated takedown directives directly to intermediaries under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, the portal structurally excludes citizens and impacted users from the grievance process.

We demand that the government introduce strictly judicially enforceable transparency requirements, publish all blocking orders, and restore the principles of natural justice to India's platform governance framework. Based on requests from our community we will also next week launch a rough public sheet in which social media users can input and add information on digital censorship.

Two members of Congress have been quietly merging two separate site-blocking bills into one.

Representative Zoe Lofgren (D) of California and Senator Thom Tillis (R) of North Carolina's bill would let copyright holders petition federal courts to order American internet service providers and DNS resolvers to block entire foreign domains.

Comcast. Verizon. Spectrum. T-Mobile. Cloudflare. Google. OpenDNS. All of them, ordered to refuse to resolve a domain on the strength of a court order obtained by the MPA's lawyers.

Once the law exists, any foreign domain a federal judge finds objectionable disappears from the address book of every American household that does not run its own resolver.

This is what fourteen years of post-SOPA institutional memory loss looks like.

In 2012, the Stop Online Piracy Act died on the floor of Congress because the public found out what was in it before it passed. Wikipedia went dark in protest. Reddit went dark. Google put a black censor bar across its homepage. The bill sponsors retreated. The lesson the entertainment industry took from that defeat was not that the public opposed internet censorship. The lesson was that public attention was the problem.

So this time the bill has been drafted in private. There has been no blackout. There has been no consumer-facing campaign. The strategy is to negotiate the details quietly with the parties most able to refuse, and the public never finds out the law exists until they cannot reach a website.

In early 2026, the Supreme Court ruled in Cox Communications v. Sony Music that an ISP cannot be held liable for a billion dollars because some of its customers downloaded music. Justice Sotomayor, in a concurrence, complained that the ruling now permits ISPs to sell internet access to "every single infringer who wants one" without lifting a finger to prevent infringement. The publishers and the studios read that as a green light to ask Congress for the lever the courts no longer hand them.

This is the lever they want. A federal court order. A list of foreign domains. ISPs and DNS resolvers compelled by law to block on receipt.

The list of countries that already have laws like this includes the United Kingdom, France, Italy, Spain, Australia, India, Brazil, and Russia. The MPA cites this as evidence that the United States is behind. In Spain, IP-level blocking ordered by the football league has knocked legitimate businesses offline because they happened to share a server with a blocked domain. In Italy, the Piracy Shield system has blocked Cloudflare entirely on multiple occasions. In the United Kingdom, blocking orders have been used to take down sites that were not piracy sites at all, on the basis that they linked to piracy sites.

The collateral damage is the system working as designed. The blunter the instrument, the easier the enforcement.

There is no version of this law that targets only the bad actors. Domains are not isolated. Hosting is shared. CDNs are shared. The address book is a single document. Once the law exists, the list of blocked domains will only grow, the criteria will only loosen, and the appeal process will only formalize what was already done.

Anything that depends on resolving a foreign domain becomes contingent on the goodwill of a federal court and the lobbying budget of whoever wants the domain alive. Every shadow library, every IPTV mirror, every privacy-respecting service whose lawyers cannot match Disney's. All of them will be one petition away from disappearing from the address book of every household whose internet runs through Comcast.

Most people do not run a VPN, do not configure a custom DNS, do not know what an IP address is. Most people get the internet their ISP serves them. The bill is written for those people. The bill assumes that if the road is closed at the resolver, the destination effectively does not exist.

This bill will outlive its sponsors, its pretext, and the industries that bought it. Laws granting infrastructure-level censorship power do not get repealed. They get expanded. Every kill switch finds a hand.

In 2002, Gujarat CM Narendra Modi sat in front of a BBC camera and admitted his one real weakness:
“One area where I was very, very weak… that was how to handle the media.”

He never forgot that lesson. He just decided the media should never be allowed to become a problem again.

When dissent is treated as a security threat and protest as a crime, the media is no longer a watchdog. It is just another department to be controlled.
The 2002 admission was honest.

The 2026 response is the real story. 68 seconds.

*STATEMENT: Escalating Digital Censorship in India*

*New Delhi, February 28, 2026*

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by a cluster of online blocking and takedown actions and ISP level service disruptions reported between 24–28 February 2026. Across these incidents, users and affected services face restrictions without clear, timely reasons and without access to the underlying orders needed to challenge state action by exercising their rights to obtain legal remedy.

Developers reported severe, uneven disruption in access to Supabase across multiple Indian networks. Reporting indicates the disruption followed a government direction, with accounts suggesting use of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Yet there has been no public statement of the grounds, scope, or duration, and no accessible order for those impacted. Supabase has publicly stated that its domains became inaccessible due to a “ministry order”, and users have been pushed to workarounds such as alternative DNS or VPNs. In parallel, users on X (formerly Twitter) continue to receive “withheld in India” notices restricting specific posts within the country. Such notices usually do not provide the government order or its reasoning. Hence, for those who are being censored the basics of natural justice of a notice, opportunity for a hearing and remedy are delayed or absent.

This is enabled by secrecy built into the blocking framework. Section 69A is implemented through the 2009 Blocking Rules, which contemplate a committee process and, where feasible, notice to intermediaries and identifiable originators. But they also impose “strict confidentiality” over requests and actions taken. When orders and reasons are secret by default, affected persons cannot test legality, necessity, proportionality, or factual errors except through protracted litigation. When in _Shreya Singhal v. Union of India_ (2015), the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A while relying on the existence of procedural safeguards and reasoned decisions, indicating that impacted users could approach court in writ remedies. However, due to the operational secrecy and providing copies of orders and notices those who are censored and prevented from obtaining judicial remedy.

The February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules, 2021 further increase these risks. The substituted Rule 3(1)(d) requires intermediaries to remove or disable access within three hours of receiving “actual knowledge”, which can arise from a court order or a written “reasoned intimation” by authorised government officers. While the rule lists what a “reasoned intimation” should contain, the legal basis, statutory provision, nature of the unlawful act, and specific URL/identifier, the three-hour window pressures platforms to comply promptly which may often occur without any substantive assessment. These inherently opaque censorship practices are being accelerated through "Sahyog" portal. Developed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the Sahyog portal operates entirely without statutory footing, only being anchored in the IT Rules, 2021 that are created by executive notification. It functions as a censorship clearinghouse that deliberately bypasses the established, albeit weak, procedural safeguards of Section 69A. By routing automated takedown directives directly to intermediaries under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, the portal structurally excludes citizens and impacted users from the grievance process.

We demand that the government introduce strictly judicially enforceable transparency requirements, publish all blocking orders, and restore the principles of natural justice to India's platform governance framework. Based on requests from our community we will also next week launch a rough public sheet in which social media users can input and add information on digital censorship.

Nearly 1.95 lakh government-backed directions to block online content were sent to Instagram, Facebook and YouTube between March and July 2026, according to data accessed by The Indian Express. That means roughly one blocking order every 68 seconds, or about 1,275 a day.

The surge came during a period that also saw student protests against exam leaks at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar, which began in early June and ended on July 25.

Instagram received the largest share, with around 1 lakh orders, followed by Facebook with about 80,000 and YouTube with nearly 15,000. A single order can cover hundreds of posts or accounts.

Most of the directions were issued by central and state government agencies, with a large number sent through the Home Ministry’s Sahyog portal. For comparison, RTI records accessed by The Indian Express showed that just 2,312 blocking orders were sent to 19 online platforms through Sahyog between October 2024 and October 2025, an average of about six a day.

The report also found that Meta has connected its systems to the Sahyog portal to meet the government’s tighter 2 to 3-hour deadline for removing flagged content. This allows directions uploaded through the system to be acted on automatically, without a separate human review by Meta, according to the report.

The scale of the increase, and the use of automated takedowns, puts a sharper focus on how India regulates content online and how platforms respond to government directions.

In domain management terms, “clientHold” is a standard EPP (Extensible Provisioning Protocol) status code controlled exclusively by the registrar, not by governments or external authorities. According to ICANN documentation and registrar policies, this status instructs the registry not to publish the domain in the DNS, effectively taking it offline until the registrar resolves the underlying issue. Such instruction can be issued only by the owner of the website, not third parties, not even governments. Alternately, the domain provider or the host can take the website offline due to various reasons.

It is commonly applied for routine administrative reasons such as incomplete WHOIS contact verification, billing or payment problems, compliance violations, or at the request of the domain owner. The clientHold affects resolution globally at the registry level, not at any country level.

On the other hand, when a government orders blocking a website, it is done through ISPs (Internet Service Providers) in the country, and the block only takes place in that country. Clear difference between Brazil and India on X regard to the open source X:

🇧🇷 Brazil • Type: Hardcoded filter in the open-source algorithm • What it is: Public ranking rule written into the code (Brazil2026ElectionFilter) • Visibility: Fully visible and inspectable in the GitHub repo • Effect: Affects “For You” recommendations (unless you already follow the account) • Scope: Official election-related candidate/campaign accounts (~665 TSE-listed for 2026)

Brazil’s election law requires platforms that use recommendation systems to treat official candidate accounts this way. X implemented it as transparent, auditable code.

🇮🇳 India • Type: Individual legal requests / orders • What it is: Case-by-case legal notices (mainly Section 69A of the IT Act) • Visibility: Specific notices and lists are mostly confidential under Indian law • Effect: Usually withholds content only inside India • Scope: Any content the government deems a threat to sovereignty, security, or public order

India has no equivalent hardcoded ranking filter in the open-source algorithm. It relies on traditional legal takedown/withholding orders.

Filters (hardcoded in open-source X algorithm) → Currently only Brazil (Brazil2026ElectionFilter)
Requests (government content removal / withholding demands)
 These are standard legal notices. X reviews them and publishes aggregate numbers in its Transparency Reports.

Highest volume (H2 2024 data from the 2025 Transparency Report): • Japan — by far the largest (69,186). Mostly local criminal laws (fraud, “yami-baito” recruitment, drugs, prostitution) • Turkey — 11,107 • South Korea — 1,835 • European Union (combined) — 3,831 • All other countries (including India, Brazil, Russia, etc.) — 11,047 combined

India is a significant requester under Section 69A and the IT Rules. X publishes separate monthly compliance reports for India, but the individual orders remain largely confidential. Content is typically withheld only for users in India.

Other regular requesters include Russia, Indonesia, Malaysia, and various EU states. None currently have a Brazil-style public filter in the open-source recommendation code.

Summary • Filters = Brazil only (visible in the code) • Requests = Many countries, with Japan, Turkey, South Korea, and India among the more active. These are handled through the normal legal process + aggregate transparency reporting, outside the open-source algorithm.

USA on X: Government Requests – Current vs Pre-Elon

🇺🇸 Current (post-Elon X, H2 2024 / 2025 Transparency Report)
 • Type: Almost entirely information/account-data requests (subpoenas, court orders, emergency disclosures). Formal content removal/withholding orders are rare. • Visibility: Aggregate numbers published in Transparency Reports. Individual requests often notified to users (unless legally prohibited). No hardcoded ranking filter in the open-source algorithm.
 • Volume: – Information requests: 3,788 (highest single country), 2,975 disclosed (78.5% rate) – Removal/withholding requests: Not broken out separately — sits inside “All Others” (~11,047 combined across dozens of countries). Japan alone accounts for ~69,000.
 • Effect: Content is almost never geo-withheld solely because the US government asks. Actions happen mainly for clear illegal content under US law or X’s own rules.
 • Scope: Criminal investigations, national security process, court orders. First Amendment sharply limits government ability to demand pure content takedowns.
Pre-Elon (Twitter, 2019–2021 reports)
 • Information requests: Also frequently the top single country (examples: ~3,026 in H1 2021 ≈ 24% of global volume, ~68% compliance; H2 2021 ≈ 20% of global, ~69% compliance). Volumes in the same ballpark as today.
 • Removal/legal demands from the US: Consistently low volume (often dozens or low hundreds at most per half-year). Global removal totals were lower overall (~40–47k per half-year).
 • Content moderation frequently involved informal government flagging and pressure (documented in the Twitter Files — FBI and other agencies routinely sent “requests” or flagged content for review under Twitter’s TOS, outside formal legal process).
Key differences (current vs pre-Elon)
 • Formal US removal/withholding volume: Remained low in both eras (First Amendment constraint).
 • Global context: Total worldwide removal requests roughly doubled post-acquisition, driven almost entirely by non-US countries (Japan, Turkey, etc.). Overall compliance rates on formal requests rose (~70–82% vs ~30–50% range pre-Elon).
 • Transparency & process: Pre-Musk had regular reports but significant informal channels. Post-Musk: reports resumed after a gap, open-sourced algorithm (only Brazil currently has a public government-required ranking filter), stronger user-notification policy, public challenges to some overbroad foreign orders, and stated rejection of secret deals.
 • Internal moderation: Pre-Elon heavier proactive enforcement on political, COVID, and election-related speech under broad TOS policies. Current approach is narrower (“freedom of speech, not reach”).

Summary The USA is the opposite of Brazil (hardcoded public ranking filter) and India (high-volume confidential Section 69A-style withholding).
 • High activity on information/data requests (stable volume, somewhat higher formal disclosure rate now).
 • Very low activity on formal content removal requests (both pre- and post-Elon).
 Main shifts under X: greater formal transparency, reduced informal pressure channels, and open visibility of any systemic ranking rules when they exist.

Sources: X 2025 Transparency Report (H2 2024 data), historical Twitter Transparency Reports (2019–2021), and public Twitter Files disclosures.

SEVEN YEARS SINCE ARTICLE 370:
THE DAY KASHMIR CHANGED DIRECTION
Seven years ago, on 5 August 2019, Jammu and Kashmir underwent the most consequential constitutional reorganisation in its recent history.

The decision was immediately surrounded by anger, apprehension, predictions of permanent instability and declarations that Kashmir would never recover.

Seven years later, the argument must no longer be conducted through slogans.

It must be tested through outcomes.

> What disappeared?
> What emerged?
> What changed on the street?
> What reached the village?
> What entered the economy?
> And what still remains unfinished?

The honest answer is that 5 August was not a magic switch that transformed Kashmir overnight.
It was a structural reset.

It dismantled an exceptional political arrangement that had gradually become the protective vocabulary of dynastic entitlement, institutional ambiguity, separatist mobilisation and permanent emotional blackmail.

For decades, Kashmir was presented as a society that could only be administered through fear, negotiated with through shutdowns and represented through a handful of political families and separatist intermediaries.

The ordinary Kashmiri rarely controlled that narrative.
The gunman claimed to speak for him.
The separatist issued calendars in his name.
The politician traded his sentiment.
The propagandist exported his suffering.
And the shopkeeper, student, labourer and parent paid the bill.

THE STREET HAS CHANGED

In 2018, Jammu and Kashmir recorded 1,328 incidents of organised stone-pelting and 52 organised hartals.

By 2023, both figures had fallen to zero. The same remained true in official data reported through July 2024.

Terrorist-initiated incidents declined from 228 in 2018 to 46 in 2023.

This is not a cosmetic improvement.

It represents the collapse of an entire infrastructure of organised disruption.
There was a time when one WhatsApp message could empty a market.
One separatist calendar could shut an entire district.
One militant funeral could mobilise thousands.
One rumour could interrupt examinations, transport, business and public life.

Kashmir’s economy was being governed not by institutions, but by uncertainty.

Today, the culture of compulsory shutdown has largely disappeared.

The significance is not that Kashmiris have lost their political voice.

The significance is that coercion no longer decides whether a child attends school, whether a shop opens, whether a patient reaches hospital or whether a family can earn its daily income.

That is freedom too.

But honesty also requires a warning:

Terrorism has not vanished.

The Pahalgam attack of April 2025, in which 26 people were killed, demonstrated that Pakistan-backed terrorism retains the ability to inflict pain and disrupt progress.

Therefore, the achievement is not the complete elimination of the threat.

It is the reduction of terrorism’s social command over Kashmir.

The terrorist may still attempt an attack.

But he no longer automatically controls the street after it.

FROM BOYCOTT TO THE BALLOT

For years, elections in Kashmir were conducted under the shadow of boycott calls, threats, selective violence and claims that voting represented betrayal.

In 2024, Jammu and Kashmir voted in its first Assembly election in a decade.

The overall turnout was 63.88%.

The elections were completed peacefully, without major election-related violence and without repolling.

That figure represents more than electoral participation.

It marks a psychological transition.

The same population that was once instructed to remain behind closed doors stepped out to elect its representatives.

The ballot did not resolve every political disagreement.

It did something more important:

It restored the ordinary citizen to the centre of politics.

Democracy replaced the separatist veto.

Political parties were forced to seek votes instead of interpreting silence.

Even parties that opposed the 2019 decision participated fully in the constitutional process created after it.

That is the great irony of post-2019 Kashmir:

Those who continue to describe the new constitutional order as illegitimate now seek authority, office and political relevance through elections held under that very order.

The boycott has ended.

The bargaining has begun.

FROM EXCEPTION TO EQUAL RIGHTS

After the constitutional changes, 170 Central laws that had not previously applied in Jammu and Kashmir were extended to the region.

These included legal protections connected with education, transparency, minority rights, domestic violence, safeguards for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, forest rights and social justice.

For the first time, constitutional protections available elsewhere in India acquired uniform legal application in Jammu and Kashmir.

This did not automatically solve every injustice.

A law written in Delhi has value only when it is implemented honestly in Kupwara, Kishtwar, Poonch, Shopian and Srinagar.

But the principle changed fundamentally:

Rights would no longer depend on whether a regional political establishment considered their application convenient.

Article 370 had been marketed as a shield protecting every Kashmiri.

In practice, it also became a wall behind which several deprived communities remained politically invisible.

Its removal did not erase Kashmiri identity.

It removed the argument that equality before national law was somehow incompatible with that identity.

THE RAILWAY MAP HAS CHANGED

The transformation is now visible in steel, tunnels and bridges.

In June 2025, the 272-kilometre Udhampur–Srinagar–Baramulla Rail Link was dedicated to the nation.

Built at an estimated cost of approximately ₹43,780 crore, the project includes:

— 36 tunnels covering around 119 kilometres
— 943 bridges
— The 359-metre-high Chenab Railway Bridge, the world’s highest railway arch bridge
— The Anji Bridge, India’s first cable-stayed railway bridge

Vande Bharat services now connect Jammu and Srinagar, reducing the journey to approximately three hours.

For generations, geography was treated as Kashmir’s permanent disadvantage.

Now engineering is beginning to convert that geography into connectivity.

An apple grower should not have to calculate his future according to a landslide.

A student should not feel nationally distant because a highway is closed.

A patient should not remain isolated by snow.

A business should not lose its market because the mountain has become impassable.

Rail connectivity is not merely infrastructure.

It is economic integration, strategic mobility and psychological proximity.

FROM AIRPORT CONGESTION TO EXPANSION

Srinagar Airport handled around 44.7 lakh passengers during FY 2024–25, despite its existing terminal being designed for a much smaller annual capacity.
In February 2026, a ₹1,677-crore expansion project was approved.
The plan is intended to increase annual passenger-handling capacity from 2.5 million to 10 million and raise peak-hour capacity from approximately 950 to 2,900 passengers.

That tells its own story.

The debate is no longer whether people will come to Kashmir.

The question is whether the infrastructure can accommodate how many are arriving.

TOURISM HAS RETURNED TO SCALE

Jammu and Kashmir recorded approximately 1.78 crore tourist arrivals in 2025, including around 36,000 foreign visitors.

These figures include different categories of visitors and pilgrimage traffic, and tourism remains vulnerable to security incidents.

Nevertheless, the direction is unmistakable.

Hotels that once calculated losses through curfew calendars now calculate occupancy.

Taxi drivers once trapped by shutdowns now depend on the length of the tourist season.

Houseboat owners, guides, artisans, restaurant workers, pony operators and small traders are again connected to a functioning visitor economy.

Earlier, instability was exported as Kashmir’s primary image.

Today, millions arrive to experience Kashmir directly.

That weakens propaganda more effectively than any press conference.

THE ECONOMY IS EXPANDING BUT MUST BECOME MORE INCLUSIVE

Jammu and Kashmir’s nominal economy is estimated at approximately ₹2.86 lakh crore in 2025–26.

Real GSDP is projected to grow by around 5.82%, while nominal growth is estimated at 8.89%.

Per-capita income is estimated at approximately ₹1.68 lakh.

The Economic Survey reports that over the preceding seven years, around 2,227 industrial units, involving investment of roughly ₹15,940 crore, became operational.

This reflects movement.

But investment announcements must not be confused with employment delivered.

A factory on a presentation slide does not provide a salary.

A memorandum of understanding is not an operational industry.

The next stage of transformation must therefore be judged by:

How many stable jobs are created?
How many local enterprises survive?
How much value is added to horticulture?
How many young people can build careers without leaving?
How many districts benefit beyond Srinagar and Jammu?

The old political economy survived by distributing government jobs, contracts and access through patronage.

The new economy must create opportunity beyond political recommendation.

Otherwise, development will remain visible in infrastructure but distant from households.

ENERGY: FROM POTENTIAL TO PRODUCTION

Major hydropower projects are now under construction, including:

— Pakal Dul: 1,000 MW
— Ratle: 850 MW
— Kiru: 624 MW
— Kwar: 540 MW

Together, these projects represent more than 3,000 MW of prospective generation capacity.

For a region with immense water resources but persistent power shortages, this is both opportunity and indictment.

Kashmir cannot indefinitely celebrate generation projects while households experience winter cuts.

The real success will come when hydropower is reflected not only in national capacity, but also in reliable local supply, fair benefits and visible economic returns.

THE MOST IMPORTANT TRANSFORMATION IS PSYCHOLOGICAL

The deepest change cannot be measured only in bridges, tourists or investment.

It lies in what Kashmir’s new generation now considers normal.
A generation once trained to recognize protest calendars is now discussing start-ups, examinations, sport, cinema, tourism, technology and entrepreneurship.
The romantic vocabulary of militancy has weakened.
The social prestige attached to street confrontation has declined.
Parents increasingly recognize that political entrepreneurs who glorified sacrifice rarely sacrificed their own children.

The separatist elite promised dignity through disorder.

But ordinary Kashmiris discovered that disorder always protects the powerful and punishes the poor.

The wealthy sent their children outside.

The shopkeeper remained behind a locked shutter.

The leader delivered speeches.

The labourer lost his wage.
The propagandist gained engagement.
The Kashmiri family received a funeral.
That business model has been disrupted.

BUT TRANSFORMATION IS NOT COMPLETION

A serious defence of 5 August must not become a denial of Kashmir’s unresolved problems.

Statehood remains pending.

Unemployment continues to frustrate young people.

Drug addiction has become a grave social emergency.

Power shortages remain unacceptable.

Recruitment processes require greater transparency.

Local businesses need protection against unequal competition.

Governance must become more accountable.

Terror networks continue to search for vulnerabilities.

And democratic institutions must be strengthened—not managed from a distance.

Peace cannot merely mean the absence of stones.

It must mean the presence of justice, opportunity, representation and responsive government.

Security created the space.

Politics and governance must now fill it.

SEVEN YEARS LATER

Before 2019, Kashmir was too often measured through:

=> Shutdown days.
=> Stone-pelting incidents.
=> Militant funerals.
=> Internet suspensions.
=> Boycott percentages.
=> Civilian casualties.
=> And economic losses.

Today, the conversation increasingly revolves around:

=> Voter turnout.
=> Tourist arrivals.
=> Rail connectivity.
=> Airport capacity.
=> Industrial units.
=> Investment.
=> Infrastructure.
=> And opportunity.

That is the transformation.

Not perfection.

Not the end of every conflict.

Not the disappearance of every grievance.

But a decisive change in direction.

5 August did not take Kashmir away from its identity.

It took away the monopoly of those who claimed that Kashmir’s identity could survive only through isolation, exceptionalism and endless instability.

Seven years later, the old ecosystem still mourns the loss of its political currency.

But Kashmir is no longer obliged to mourn with it.

The Valley has moved from enforced silence to democratic participation.

From shutdown calendars to train timetables.

From stone-pelting statistics to tourism figures.

From emotional exploitation to economic aspiration.

From a conflict managed by intermediaries to a future increasingly claimed by ordinary people.

5 August 2019 was not the day Kashmir lost its future.

It was the day those who had monopolized Kashmir’s future began losing control over it.

The transformation is visible.

The responsibility now is to deepen it, democratize it and ensure that its benefits reach every household.

Because the final measure of a new Kashmir will not be how loudly governments celebrate the change.

It will be how fully ordinary Kashmiris experience it.

DigiLocker is safer than a plastic folder — unless you download the fake app

On 29 November 2025, the official Digital India handle posted a warning that should have been louder than it was. Fraudulent apps with names like DigiLocker were circulating on app stores. The instruction was blunt: use only the authentic DigiLocker application. If you had already installed a suspicious version, delete it and change the passwords on linked accounts.

Moneycontrol reported the advisory the next day. Times of India followed for students. This is the incident. I am not going to invent a victim. The government warning is the case.

Why a plastic folder loses

A plastic folder can be stolen, soaked, or left on a bus. DigiLocker is safer than that folder for a simple reason. It is not a photo album of papers you scanned. It is a wallet that government issuers can push documents into.

The official site is https://t.co/kNUXgk5XJe. From there you can access, share, and get government-issued documents verified: a driving licence, a vehicle RC, marksheets, and other records the issuer has actually placed in your account.

How it works, without the brochure language

You open an account that is authenticated with Aadhaar. Then an RTO, a school board, a university, or another issuer sends a digitally signed document into that account. When a verifier checks it, they are not squinting at a JPEG you uploaded. They are looking at the issuer's signature.

That is why a screenshot is not the same thing. A screenshot is a picture. An issued DigiLocker document is a signed record from the source. You can crop a marksheet photo in two minutes. You cannot forge the issuer's signature by taking a better photo.

MeitY has been clear on the legal point. Issued documents in DigiLocker are deemed at par with originals. The official about page says the same thing under the IT Act, and in more formal language under Rule 9A of the 2016 Digital Locker rules. You can show a digital driving licence, or pull a Class X or Class XII marksheet, without laminating another photocopy.

That legal status is useful only if you are inside the real locker.

The live warning

A clone that looks like DigiLocker does not need to "hack the government." It only needs you to type an Aadhaar number and share an OTP. DigiLocker does not make you unhackable. The risk moved. Paper used to get lost. Now someone tries to phish the OTP that opens the locker.

The authentic app is published by the National e-Governance Division (NeGD), Government of India. The official website is https://t.co/kNUXgk5XJe. Install from there, or from the store listing that site points to. Confirm the developer name before you tap Install.

Do not install from a forwarded WhatsApp link. Do not trust a search ad that says "DigiLocker KYC" and asks for an OTP on a random page. No genuine officer needs that code from you on a link they just sent.

If a suspicious version is already on the phone, do what the advisory said. Delete it. Change the passwords on linked accounts. Then install the real app and check which documents are actually sitting there.

What to do before you need it

Before a road trip, open the real app and pull your driving licence and RC. Do it at home, on your own Wi-Fi, while you are not being rushed by a checkpoint or a rental desk.

Before admissions or a job file, students can pull marksheets from the board instead of hunting a laminated copy. If a verifier will accept DigiLocker, give them the issued document, not a crop of your screen.

Never share an OTP for "DigiLocker KYC" on a random link. The locker is tied to Aadhaar. The OTP is the key. Anyone who wants the key on a page you did not open from https://t.co/AE2sh860xw is not helping you file a document.

If you already downloaded something that only looked official, treat it as a live problem, not an embarrassing mistake. Delete the app. Change passwords. Watch bank and Aadhaar-linked SMS for a few days. Then start again from the official site.

The honest limit

A plastic folder fails when you lose it. DigiLocker fails when you hand the key to a lookalike. The folder is still worse for rain. The lookalike is worse for everything else.

Use the real locker. Pull the issued document, not a screenshot. Keep the OTP to yourself. That is the whole guide.

This article is written for general education and is not legal advice. It does not claim DigiLocker cannot be abused. The risk moved from lost paper to phishing for your Aadhaar OTP.

Sources: DigiLocker official site https://t.co/T2NXjM8lAm; DigiLocker About (issued documents at par with originals, IT Act / Rule 9A); MeitY statement that issued DigiLocker documents are deemed at par with originals; Digital India on X, 29 Nov 2025, authentic-app warning; Moneycontrol, 30 Nov 2025, fake DigiLocker apps advisory; Times of India Education, 11 Dec 2025, student guidance to use official sources.
